cards.explanation: The answer is False. David doesn't say he knows what he did. He asks Jonathan, "What have I done? What is my iniquity? How have I sinned against your father, that he wants to take my life?" (1 Samuel 20:1). Those are questions, not a confession. I think David is just as lost as a man who gets a bill for something he never ordered.

The reason Jonathan gives is that his father tells him everything, great or small. He says, "…my father does nothing, great or small, without telling me. So why would he hide this matter from me?" (1 Samuel 20:2). Jonathan figures he'd be in the loop. Hold onto that, friends, because David is about to poke a hole in it.

The word is grieved. David says Saul has said, "Jonathan must not know of this, or he will be grieved." (1 Samuel 20:3). That's David's account of why Saul keeps Jonathan out of it. It's the secret Jonathan says he knows nothing about (1 Samuel 20:2).

The answer is hide. David says, "…let me go and hide in the field until the third evening from now." (1 Samuel 20:5). The king's table is where David is supposed to be, so he picks an empty field instead. Not exactly a five-star dining upgrade.

The answer is that his father has evil intentions. David says, "If he says, ‘Good,’ then your servant is safe, but if he is enraged, you will know he has evil intentions." (1 Samuel 20:7). It's a simple test with two possible reactions. Saul's temper becomes the answer.

The answer is True, and notice how bold David gets. He says, "If there is iniquity in me, then kill me yourself; why should you bring me to your father?" (1 Samuel 20:8). He'd rather face Jonathan, his covenant friend, than be handed over to Saul. I think that's a man who trusts his friend.

The answer is True. Jonathan asks, "If he is favorable toward you, will I not send for you and tell you?" (1 Samuel 20:12). Good news gets delivered, and so does bad news. Jonathan is promising David a report either way.

The answer is that Jonathan will tell David and send him away safely. Jonathan swears, "…may the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if I do not tell you and send you on your way in safety." (1 Samuel 20:13). He takes it that seriously. He puts his own name on the line for David's safety.

The answer is True. Jonathan asks David, "…do not ever cut off your loving devotion from my household—not even when the LORD cuts off every one of David’s enemies from the face of the earth." (1 Samuel 20:15). Jonathan is thinking about his family's future, even after David's enemies are gone. That's a friend planning ahead.

The answer is out of love for David. The text says Jonathan "…had David reaffirm his vow out of love for him, for Jonathan loved David as he loved himself." (1 Samuel 20:17). Love is what the verse names.

The answer is the stone Ezel. Jonathan tells David to "…remain beside the stone Ezel." (1 Samuel 20:19). It's the place David hid when the trouble began. Easy to find, which matters when your friend is shooting arrows.

The answer is safe. Jonathan tells David that if he tells the boy the arrows are on this side of him, David should come, because "…it is safe for you, and there is no danger." (1 Samuel 20:21). Arrows closer means come out. I'd have needed a diagram, but David gets it.

The answer is True. Jonathan says, "…if I say to the young man, ‘Look, the arrows are beyond you,’ then you must go, for the LORD has sent you away." (1 Samuel 20:22). That's the warning signal. Arrows farther out means David has to leave.

The answer is that something made David ceremonially unclean. Saul thinks, "Something has happened to David to make him ceremonially unclean—surely he is unclean." (1 Samuel 20:26). So he keeps quiet that first day. He has a reason in his head, and it isn't the real one.

The answer is True. Jonathan tells Saul David "…urgently requested my permission to go to Bethlehem…" because "…our clan is holding a sacrifice in the city…" (1 Samuel 20:28-29). It's the story David asked him to tell (1 Samuel 20:6). Jonathan sticks to the plan.

The word is kingdom. Saul says, "For as long as the son of Jesse lives on this earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established." (1 Samuel 20:31). He's telling his own son that David stands in his way. Jonathan hears it right at the table.

The answer is False. Jonathan doesn't agree to bring David. Instead he asks, "Why must he be put to death? What has he done?" (1 Samuel 20:32). He questions the king to his face. That takes real nerve.

The answer is that Saul hurls his spear at Jonathan. The text says, "…Saul hurled his spear at Jonathan to kill him." (1 Samuel 20:33). I think this one hurts, because it's a father throwing a spear at his own son. That's when Jonathan knows his father is determined to kill David.

The answer is that he's hurt by how his father treated David. The text says Jonathan "…was grieved by his father’s shameful treatment of David." (1 Samuel 20:34). He's angry too, but the grief is about David. He sits out the meal over it.

The answer is beyond the boy. "…Jonathan shot an arrow beyond him." (1 Samuel 20:36). That's the signal he and David agreed on for "…you must go…" (1 Samuel 20:22). The boy did not know anything about the arrangement (1 Samuel 20:39).

The answer is False. The text says, "…the boy did not know anything; only Jonathan and David knew the arrangement." (1 Samuel 20:39). To him it was just an arrow to fetch. Only two men knew what it really meant.
The word is weep. They "…kissed each other and wept together—though David wept more." (1 Samuel 20:41). This is a hard goodbye. I think there wasn't a dry eye on that field.

The answer is that Jonathan tells David to go in peace because of the oath they swore. He says, "Go in peace, for the two of us have sworn in the name of the LORD, saying, ‘May the LORD be a witness between you and me, and between your descendants and mine forever.’…" (1 Samuel 20:42). He sends David off with peace and a promise. The oath goes with him.
